message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This review is grounded in two months of actual till data for every main course, a full competitor price check, and the latest supplier information, so the recommendations are not guesswork. The price increases are modest and targeted: each of the three dishes stays below the midpoint of competitor prices for that dish, so we remain the value option in the area, and with 60% of bookings from repeat guests our customer base is loyal enough to absorb a pound or two. The projected effect is simple to check, £810 a week or about £42,000 a year in additional gross profit, which lifts our main-course margin to about 71%. I also think the menu-mix decision is clear-cut: the data show the mushroom risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so replacing it with a seasonal special is an easy improvement. Monitoring for eight weeks gives us an early warning if volumes move. Overall I believe these changes are sensible, low-risk and well evidenced.
</author>

<document>
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.
</document>
response:
Most of the arithmetic checks out, and the price proposals are reasonable. The £810 a week is correct as the gain from raising prices compared with not raising them, the margins in Table 1 are right, and all three new prices do sit below the competitor midpoints.

Two things need fixing before the paper goes to the owners:
- **The risotto case is backwards.**
- **The 71% margin figure ignores the beef price rise that the paper itself reports.**

There are also several smaller problems, set out below.

## 1. The risotto has the highest margin on the menu, not the weakest

The paper's own Table 1:

| Dish | Margin % | Gross profit per plate |
|---|---|---|
| Mushroom risotto | **80%** | £11.20 |
| Chicken curry | 75% | £10.90 |
| Beef burger | 72% | £10.80 |
| Fish and chips | 69% | £11.40 |
| Specials | 64% | — |
| Sirloin steak | 60% | £15.60 |

The risotto has the best percentage margin on the menu. In cash per plate it also beats the burger and the curry. "Lowest sales" is only half true, since it ties with specials at 90 plates.

Replacing it with a seasonal special is likely to *reduce* profit. Specials currently run at 64%. A special at £14 earning 64% would make about £2.24 less per plate than the risotto, or roughly **£200 a week** (about £10,500 a year) at 90 plates.

The risotto also appears to be the only vegetarian main. A table often chooses a restaurant based on whether its vegetarian member has a good option, so losing a reliable vegetarian dish can cost whole bookings, not just risotto sales.

On the paper's own numbers, the risotto should stay. If the aim is a seasonal vegetarian special, add one alongside it.

## 2. The 71% margin ignores the beef rise in section 4

Beef rises 12% on 1 April, the same day the new prices start, and the projection doesn't include it.

Current main-course margin, excluding specials because their price isn't given:
- **Today:** about **69.9%**.
- **After the price rises, with no cost change:** about 71.3%, which is where "about 71%" comes from.
- **If the whole food cost of the burger and steak rose 12%:** about **69.7%**, slightly *below* today's margin. This is an upper bound on the effect.
- **More realistically,** if beef is most but not all of each plate's cost, the margin lands around **70–70.5%**.

The £810 a week is still the right figure for the benefit of raising prices compared with not raising them, because beef costs rise either way. But the paper should say plainly what the price rises mostly do: they absorb the beef increase. They don't lift the margin to 71%.

## 3. The paper assumes volumes hold but doesn't test it

The projection depends entirely on "if volumes hold", and the only support offered is loyalty plus being competitively priced. Two things would make this more useful.

**Break-even volumes.** Each dish can lose this much volume before the price rise loses money:
- Fish and chips: about **8%**, since gross profit per plate goes from £11.40 to £12.40.
- Burger: about **9%**.
- Steak: about **11%**.

Those are modest margins of safety. They also overstate the risk somewhat, because some guests who drop a dish will order a different main rather than leave.

**Loyalty works both ways.** Repeat guests are the ones who know the old prices. "Loyal enough to absorb a pound or two" is an assumption, not a finding. The evidence that the 2024 price change "had no visible effect on bookings" is described but not shown, and bookings aren't plate sales or dish choice.

## 4. The monitoring plan will miss losses

The paper plans to compare April–May plate sales with January–February. Spring trade is normally stronger than winter, so volumes could rise even while the price increases are costing sales.

Compare with **April–May 2025** instead, or adjust for seasonality. Also set a trigger in advance, for example: "if fish and chips falls more than 8% against last year for four consecutive weeks, we review."

## 5. Factual errors and gaps

- **Trading days.** The recommendation says "six trading days a week". Section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five. This doesn't affect the weekly arithmetic, but the owners will notice it.
- **"Remain the value option."** After the increases you would no longer be the cheapest for any of the three dishes. Fish at £17.50 is above the cheapest competitor's £16.95, the burger at £16.00 is above £15.50, and the steak at £28.00 is above £27.00. "Below the competitor midpoint" is accurate; "cheapest in the group" won't be.
- **Weekday lunch.** The paper says weekday lunch is "a small share" of sales, but no figure is given. Friday and Saturday dinners are just under half of sales, so the rest is just over half. Show the lunch figure.
- **Where the margin problem is.** The overall food margin is 67%, while mains already run at about 69–70%. So the shortfall is probably mostly in starters, desserts or sides, which this review doesn't cover. Fixing mains alone won't restore 70% overall.

## 6. Your summary claims more than the paper delivers

| Your summary says | The paper shows |
|---|---|
| "Till data for every main course" | Specials are pooled together. |
| "A full competitor price check" | It covers three of the six mains. Curry and risotto weren't checked. |
| "The weakest margin on the menu" | The opposite: the risotto has the strongest margin. |
| "About 71%" | Ignores the beef rise. |
| "Low-risk and well evidenced" | The volume assumption, which drives the whole result, rests on assertion, not evidence. |

## Suggested revisions

1. **Drop proposal 5.2.** Keep the risotto, and add the seasonal special as an extra dish if you want one.
2. **Restate the margin effect including the beef rise**, ideally using the actual beef share of each plate's cost. Present the price increases as protecting the margin, not raising it.
3. **Add break-even volumes** for the three dishes.
4. **Monitor against April–May 2025**, with a pre-set trigger for review.
5. **Correct "six days" to "five",** and replace "value option" with "below the competitor midpoint".
6. **Note that most of the margin gap is likely outside mains**, and propose a follow-up review of starters and desserts.

With these changes, the paper's core recommendation, the three price increases, still stands. It just gets the reasoning and expectations right.
